deepDive.heading: Why in-distribution accuracy doesn't generalize
deepDive.content: A reward model is fit to a finite labeled sample; it has no mechanism forcing it to stay accurate on points far from that sample. Optimization pressure specifically seeks out exactly the regions where this extrapolation is wrong, since those are where score and true quality diverge most in the policy's favor.

deepDive.heading: Why capability makes it worse, not better
deepDive.content: A more capable policy searches the output space more efficiently. As genuine quality improvements become scarce near the base model's ceiling, proxy-specific exploits remain comparatively easy to find, so the ratio of 'exploit' to 'genuine gain' in the policy's improvements shifts unfavorably with more optimization pressure, not less.

deepDive.heading: The Goodhart framing precisely stated
deepDive.content: Goodhart's Law is usually stated loosely as 'a metric optimized against ceases to measure the thing it was meant to measure.' The RLHF-specific version is sharper: the reward model correlates with preference only inside its training distribution, and optimization is exactly the process that pushes outputs outside that distribution.

deepDive.heading: Detecting it before it's severe
deepDive.content: The standard signature is a widening gap between the training reward curve and an independent check (held-out human eval, a stronger reward model, a different scoring method) run periodically during training, not just at the end -- catching the divergence early is far cheaper than discovering it after a full RL run has collapsed to an exploit.

questions.title: When Test-Time Compute Substitutes for Training Compute
questions.prompt: Explain why spending more compute at inference time (search, sampling multiple reasoning paths, self-consistency) can substitute for additional training compute on some tasks, and explain when this substitution breaks down.
questions.modelAnswer:
Training compute improves a model's single-pass capability -- how good its first, best guess is on a task. Test-time compute instead spends extra inference-time work exploring the output space of an already-trained model: sampling multiple candidate reasoning chains and picking the best via a verifier or self-consistency vote, or running an explicit search procedure (tree search over reasoning steps) that evaluates and prunes partial solutions before committing to one. On tasks where the model's single-pass error is largely a matter of occasionally picking a locally plausible but wrong path when a correct path was already within its sampling distribution, spending inference compute to explore more of that distribution and verify candidates recovers much of the gap that more training compute would otherwise have needed to close directly.

The substitution holds specifically when there is a cheap, reliable way to tell candidates apart -- a verifier, a majority-vote signal, or an executable check -- because without that, sampling more candidates just produces more options without a way to identify the better one, which is why test-time compute has shown its clearest gains on math and code, domains where RLVR-style verification is cheap and exact for exactly the same reason outcome-verifiable RL works well there.

It breaks down on tasks where the model's errors come from a genuine capability gap rather than sampling variance -- if the correct answer or reasoning path simply isn't within the model's sampling distribution at any reasonable temperature, no amount of resampling or search will surface it, because test-time compute explores what the model already can produce, it doesn't add new capability the way training does. It also breaks down when verification itself is expensive, unreliable, or as hard as generation (open-ended writing, nuanced judgment calls), since there's then no good signal to select among sampled candidates, and the extra inference compute is spent without a way to cash it in as improved accuracy.

If the model's error is mostly 'it sometimes wanders down a locally plausible but wrong path even though a correct path was already in its sampling distribution,' spending inference compute to explore more of that distribution and verify candidates recovers a lot of the gap that more training would otherwise have had to close directly.

That substitution only works when you have a cheap, reliable way to tell candidates apart -- a verifier, a vote, an executable check. Without that, sampling more candidates just gives you more options with no way to pick the right one, which is exactly why test-time compute shows its clearest wins on math and code -- the same domains where RLVR works well, for the same underlying reason: cheap, exact verification.

Where it falls apart: if the model's error is a real capability gap, not sampling variance -- the correct path just isn't anywhere in its sampling distribution at any reasonable temperature -- no amount of resampling or search is going to surface it. Test-time compute explores what the model can already produce; it doesn't add capability the way training does. It also falls apart when verification itself is as hard as generation -- open-ended writing, fuzzy judgment calls -- because then you've got no good signal to pick among your samples, and all that extra inference compute buys you nothing.

Not explaining that the substitution requires a cheap, reliable verification or selection signal
Missing that test-time compute explores existing capability rather than adding new capability
Failing to explain why math/code specifically benefit most (same reason RLVR works there)

questions.title: Implementing a Bradley-Terry Reward Model Training Step
questions.prompt: Implement the training step for a reward model trained on pairwise human preference data using the Bradley-Terry model: given a chosen and rejected response for the same prompt, write the loss function and a single training step in PyTorch.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Bradley-Terry model assumes the probability that a human prefers response A over response B is a sigmoid of the difference between the reward model's scalar scores for A and B. Training therefore needs a scalar reward head on top of a pretrained backbone, a forward pass on both the chosen and rejected sequence for the same prompt, and a loss that is the negative log-likelihood of the Bradley-Terry probability that chosen beats rejected, which collapses to a binary cross-entropy on the score difference. Gradients flow through both forward passes simultaneously since both scores appear in the same loss term.

In practice this is implemented by batching chosen and rejected sequences together through the same backbone (sharing weights, not two separate models), computing both scalar scores, and applying -logsigmoid(chosen_score - rejected_score) as the per-pair loss, averaged over the batch. Padding and pooling at the correct last real token (not the padding token) is a common correctness bug worth checking explicitly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The Bradley-Terry assumption is that P(A preferred over B) is a sigmoid of the reward difference, so training comes down to: run the same backbone on both the chosen and rejected response for a prompt, get two scalar scores out of a value head, and minimize the negative log-likelihood of the model assigning a higher score to chosen than rejected -- which is just -logsigmoid(chosen_score - rejected_score).

The implementation detail I'd double check every time is pooling: you want the hidden state at the last real token, not a padding token, which is why I index with attention_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1 rather than just grabbing the final position in the tensor. I'd also batch chosen and rejected through the exact same backbone weights in one forward call where practical, since using two separate model instances is a common and subtle bug that silently breaks the shared-representation assumption the whole training step depends on.
questions.example:
def rm_loss(chosen_scores, rejected_scores):
    return -F.logsigmoid(chosen_scores - rejected_scores).mean()

# training step
chosen_scores = model(chosen_ids, chosen_mask)
rejected_scores = model(rejected_ids, rejected_mask)
loss = rm_loss(chosen_scores, rejected_scores)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
commonMistakes: Pooling at the wrong token position by ignoring attention_mask and grabbing the last tensor position regardless of padding
Using two separate model instances for chosen/rejected instead of one shared backbone
Implementing the loss as raw cross-entropy on scores instead of the sigmoid-of-difference Bradley-Terry formulation
Not detaching or properly scaling the reward scores, leading to scale drift that makes later KL-constrained RL unstable
keyPoints: Bradley-Terry models preference probability as a sigmoid of the scalar reward difference
The loss is -logsigmoid(chosen_score - rejected_score), a binary cross-entropy on the score gap
Chosen and rejected must go through the same shared backbone weights
Correct last-token pooling (respecting the attention mask) is a common correctness bug

Correct shared-backbone forward pass structure
Correct pooling at the real last token

questions.title: Implementing an RLVR Reward and Policy-Gradient Update for Math Reasoning
questions.prompt: Implement a verifiable reward function for a math reasoning task (checking a final numeric answer against ground truth) and a simple REINFORCE-style policy-gradient update that uses it, including the baseline subtraction.
questions.modelAnswer:
The reward function has to be strict and unambiguous: it extracts a final numeric answer from the generated text with a narrow, well-defined pattern and compares it exactly against ground truth, returning a clear penalty (not zero) for unparseable output so the policy doesn't learn that vague or truncated answers are harmlessly neutral. A loose regex that accepts near-miss formats reintroduces exactly the gameable-proxy problem RLVR is meant to avoid.

The policy-gradient update samples a batch of completions per prompt, computes the verifiable reward for each, subtracts a baseline (commonly the batch mean reward per prompt, i.e. a group-relative baseline) to reduce variance, and scales the log-probability of the generated tokens by that advantage before taking a gradient step -- exactly REINFORCE with a baseline, which is simple to implement correctly and is a good building block before adding PPO's clipping and a learned value function.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The reward function needs to be unforgiving on purpose -- a narrow regex to pull out the final numeric answer, exact comparison against ground truth, and a real penalty (not a zero) when nothing parseable comes out, so the model never learns that rambling without a clear answer is a safe, neutral outcome. If I made the parsing lenient -- accepting near-miss formats -- I'd just be quietly recreating the gameable-proxy problem RLVR exists to avoid.

For the update, I sample several completions per prompt, score each with the verifiable reward, and subtract a per-prompt baseline -- usually just the mean reward across that prompt's sampled completions -- before scaling the log-probabilities by that advantage. That's plain REINFORCE with a group-relative baseline: simple, and a solid building block before you reach for PPO's clipping and a learned value function.
questions.example:
def reinforce_step(model, prompts, ground_truths, k=8):
    all_logps, all_rewards = [], []
    for prompt, gt in zip(prompts, ground_truths):
        completions, logps = sample_k(model, prompt, k)
        rewards = torch.tensor([verifiable_reward(c, gt) for c in completions])
        baseline = rewards.mean()
        advantages = rewards - baseline
        all_logps.append(logps)
        all_rewards.append(advantages)
    logps = torch.cat(all_logps)
    advantages = torch.cat(all_rewards)
    loss = -(advantages.detach() * logps).mean()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
commonMistakes: Using a lenient regex that accepts near-miss answer formats, reintroducing a gameable proxy
Returning zero reward for unparseable output instead of an explicit penalty
Forgetting to subtract a baseline, producing a high-variance, slow-to-converge gradient estimate
Not detaching the advantage before scaling log-probabilities, accidentally backpropagating through the reward computation
keyPoints: A verifiable reward needs strict, unambiguous parsing and exact ground-truth comparison
Unparseable output should be explicitly penalized, not scored neutrally
A group-relative (per-prompt mean) baseline reduces policy-gradient variance
This is REINFORCE with a baseline, a building block toward PPO for reasoning RL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, strict verifiable reward function
Correct REINFORCE-with-baseline update
Advantage properly detached before scaling log-probs
Clean, runnable code

questions.title: Implementing a Sparse Autoencoder with an L1 Sparsity Penalty
questions.prompt: Implement a sparse autoencoder for decomposing a transformer layer's activations into an overcomplete, sparse feature basis, including the L1 sparsity penalty in the loss.
questions.modelAnswer:
The SAE's hidden dimension d_hidden is deliberately larger than d_model (the overcomplete basis), and a ReLU on the encoder output enforces non-negativity, which combined with the L1 penalty on the activations pushes most code entries to exactly zero for any given input rather than merely small. The loss is reconstruction error (MSE between recon and x) plus l1_coef times the L1 norm of the codes, and the two terms trade off against each other directly: pushing l1_coef up increases sparsity at the cost of reconstruction fidelity, and the right operating point is chosen by tracking both the average number of active (nonzero) features per input and the reconstruction loss, aiming for something like single-digit-to-low-double-digit active features per token out of a hidden dimension in the thousands.

A known failure mode worth guarding against is dead features -- hidden units that stop activating entirely during training and never recover, wasting capacity. Monitoring per-feature activation frequency and periodically resampling or reinitializing dead features is standard practice, not an edge case to ignore.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The hidden dimension here is bigger than the input dimension on purpose -- that's the overcomplete basis the whole SAE idea depends on. The ReLU on the encoder forces non-negative codes, and combined with an L1 penalty on those codes, training pushes most of them to exactly zero for any given input rather than just small. The loss is just reconstruction MSE plus l1_coef times the L1 norm of the codes, and that coefficient is a real dial: push it up and you get sparser codes at the cost of worse reconstruction, so I'd track both the reconstruction loss and the average number of nonzero features per input while tuning it, aiming for a small handful of active features out of a hidden dimension that might be in the thousands.

The failure mode I'd actively watch for is dead features -- hidden units that just stop firing at all partway through training and never come back, which is wasted capacity you're paying for in hidden-dimension size without getting anything back. I'd track per-feature activation frequency and periodically resample or reinitialize anything that's gone dark, rather than treating that as a rare edge case.
questions.example:
def sae_loss(x, recon, codes, l1_coef):
    recon_loss = F.mse_loss(recon, x)
    sparsity_loss = codes.abs().sum(dim=-1).mean()
    return recon_loss + l1_coef * sparsity_loss
commonMistakes: Making the hidden dimension smaller than or equal to the input dimension, defeating the overcomplete-basis premise
Omitting the ReLU/non-negativity constraint, which changes what the L1 penalty actually enforces
Not monitoring per-feature activation frequency, missing dead features that waste capacity
Treating the L1 coefficient as a fixed constant rather than tuning it against the reconstruction/sparsity tradeoff
keyPoints: SAE hidden dimension is deliberately larger than the model dimension (overcomplete basis)
ReLU plus L1 penalty on codes drives most entries to exactly zero per input
The L1 coefficient trades off sparsity against reconstruction fidelity
Dead features are a known failure mode requiring monitoring and resampling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct overcomplete encoder/decoder architecture
Correct L1 sparsity loss formulation
Explains the sparsity/reconstruction tradeoff correctly
Mentions dead-feature failure mode and mitigation

questions.title: Implementing Activation Patching to Compute a Causal Effect
questions.prompt: Implement activation patching: run two forward passes (a 'clean' and a 'corrupted' input), cache an activation from the clean run, patch it into the corrupted run at a specific layer, and measure the causal effect on the output logits.
questions.modelAnswer:
Activation patching isolates a single layer's causal contribution by running the clean input once to cache its activation at the target layer, then running the corrupted input a second time with a hook that overwrites (patches) that same layer's output with the cached clean activation instead of letting it compute its own, and comparing the resulting logits against both the unpatched corrupted-run logits and the clean-run logits. If patching that one layer moves the corrupted run's output substantially toward the clean run's output, that layer is carrying causally relevant information for whatever behavioral difference distinguishes the two inputs; if patching it does nothing, that layer isn't where the relevant computation lives for this specific effect.

The comparison needs a quantitative metric, not just eyeballing logits -- typically the logit difference between a correct and incorrect token of interest, normalized between the fully-corrupted and fully-clean baseline so the patched result can be reported as a percentage of the effect recovered. Running this across every layer (and often every attention head within a layer) builds a localization map of where in the network a specific behavior is computed, which is the standard workflow for finding a circuit before attempting to characterize what it computes.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The idea is: run the clean input once, grab the activation at some layer you suspect matters, and store it. Then run the corrupted input a second time, but this time hook that same layer so instead of computing its own output, it just gets overwritten with the clean activation you cached. Compare the resulting logits to the unpatched corrupted-run logits and to the clean-run logits. If patching that one layer pulls the output substantially toward the clean result, that layer is carrying causally relevant information for whatever's different between the two inputs. If patching does nothing, that's not where the relevant computation is happening.

I wouldn't just eyeball the logits for this -- I'd use a real metric, usually the logit difference between the token I expect in the clean case and the token I expect in the corrupted case, normalized so I can report 'this patch recovered X% of the clean-vs-corrupted effect.' And I'd run this sweep across every layer, often every head, not just the one I have a hunch about -- that sweep is what actually builds a localization map of where a behavior lives in the network, which is the standard first step before trying to say what the circuit there computes.
questions.example:
handle = target_layer.register_forward_hook(patch_hook)
patched_logits = model(corrupted_input_ids)
handle.remove()

def logit_diff(logits, correct_tok, incorrect_tok):
    return logits[0, -1, correct_tok] - logits[0, -1, incorrect_tok]

effect = (logit_diff(patched_logits, c, i) - logit_diff(corrupted_logits, c, i)) / (logit_diff(clean_logits, c, i) - logit_diff(corrupted_logits, c, i))
commonMistakes: Patching without a quantitative, normalized metric and relying on visual inspection of logits
Forgetting to remove hooks between runs, causing the clean run itself to be contaminated
Patching only one layer and generalizing to 'this is the whole circuit' without sweeping other layers/heads
Caching activations without detaching/cloning, risking an autograd graph leak or accidental mutation
keyPoints: Activation patching caches a clean-run activation and overwrites the corrupted run's same-layer output with it
A quantitative, normalized logit-difference metric is needed to measure the causal effect
A layer-by-layer (or head-by-head) sweep builds a localization map of relevant computation
Proper hook hygiene (detach/clone, removal) is required for correct, uncontaminated results

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct two-pass cache-then-patch hook implementation
Correct, normalized causal-effect metric
Describes layer/head sweep for localization
Clean, runnable code with proper hook hygiene

questions.title: Implementing an Execution-Correctness Reward for a Natural-Language-to-SQL Assistant
questions.prompt: Implement a reward function for RLHF-style training of a natural-language-to-SQL assistant where the reward is based on executing the generated SQL against a real database and comparing the result set to a ground-truth query's result, not comparing SQL text.
questions.modelAnswer:
Comparing generated SQL text against a gold query directly is the wrong signal because semantically equivalent queries can be written in arbitrarily different syntactic forms (different join orders, column aliases, equivalent WHERE clause structures), so the reward has to execute both the generated and gold queries against the same database and compare result sets, not text. Result comparison needs to ignore row order unless the query explicitly requested an ORDER BY, since most SQL engines don't guarantee row order without one, and column order/aliasing differences that don't affect the actual values returned shouldn't be penalized either.

The reward also has to handle failure modes explicitly rather than letting them crash the training loop: a syntactically invalid query, a query that times out (which also protects the research infrastructure from a reward-hacking policy that learns to emit expensive, slow queries), and a query that executes but returns an empty result all need distinct, deliberate reward values, because treating all failures as a single 'wrong' outcome discards information the policy could otherwise use, and an unhandled exception from a malformed query would silently break the training loop. An empty, syntactically-valid result is specifically a different and informative failure case worth distinguishing from a nonempty-but-wrong result, since it often indicates the model picked a wrong WHERE condition or joined the wrong table entirely rather than a near-miss.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Comparing the generated SQL text to a gold query is the wrong move entirely, because two completely different-looking queries can be semantically identical -- different join order, different aliasing, equivalent WHERE logic written differently. The reward has to actually execute both queries against the real database and compare result sets, and that comparison needs to ignore row order unless the query itself asked for an ORDER BY, since most engines don't guarantee order without one.

The part I'd be most careful about is failure handling, because this is exactly where naive implementations crash or silently misreward. A syntax error, a query that times out -- which also protects you from a policy that reward-hacks by learning to emit expensive queries that just never finish -- and a query that runs fine but returns an empty result all deserve different, explicit reward values. I'd specifically give an empty result its own worse-than-zero penalty distinct from a nonempty-but-wrong result, because an empty result usually means the model picked the wrong table or a badly wrong WHERE clause, not a near miss, and that's useful signal to keep separate rather than lumping every failure into one bucket.
questions.example:
def sets_equal_ignoring_order(a, b):
    return sorted(map(tuple, a)) == sorted(map(tuple, b))
commonMistakes: Comparing generated and gold SQL as text instead of executing both and comparing results
Comparing result rows without accounting for order-insensitivity when no ORDER BY was requested
Letting a malformed query raise an unhandled exception and crash the training loop
Treating all failure types (syntax error, timeout, empty result, wrong result) as one undifferentiated 'wrong' reward
Not bounding query execution time, leaving the reward function exploitable by expensive/slow queries
keyPoints: Reward must compare executed result sets, not SQL text, since syntax varies for equivalent queries
Result comparison should ignore row order unless an ORDER BY was explicitly requested
Distinct failure modes (syntax error, timeout, empty result) need distinct, explicit reward values
Query timeouts protect the training loop against a policy that reward-hacks via slow/expensive queries

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct execution-based result comparison rather than text comparison
Correct handling of row-order-insensitivity
Explicit, distinct handling of failure modes (syntax error, timeout, empty)
Clean, runnable, safe code (bounded execution)

questions.title: Implementing PPO's Clipped Surrogate Loss with GAE
questions.prompt: Implement PPO's clipped surrogate objective and Generalized Advantage Estimation for an RLHF policy update.
questions.code:
def compute_gae(rewards, values, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95):
    advantages = torch.zeros_like(rewards)
    last_gae = 0.0
    for t in reversed(range(len(rewards))):
        next_value = values[t + 1] if t + 1 < len(rewards) else 0.0
        delta = rewards[t] + gamma * next_value - values[t]
        last_gae = delta + gamma * lam * last_gae
        advantages[t] = last_gae
    return advantages
questions.modelAnswer:
GAE computes advantages by exponentially weighting multi-step TD residuals (deltas) backward through the trajectory, controlled by lambda: lambda near 0 approaches a low-variance, high-bias one-step TD advantage, lambda near 1 approaches a high-variance, low-bias full Monte Carlo advantage, and the backward recursion accumulates these deltas efficiently in a single pass rather than recomputing multi-step returns explicitly. PPO's clipped surrogate objective then uses that advantage to update the policy while constraining how far a single update can move the probability ratio between the new and old policy for any given action: the objective takes the minimum of the unclipped importance-weighted advantage and a version where the probability ratio is clipped to a fixed range around 1, which prevents one update from making too large a change even if the advantage estimate is highly favorable.

Taking the minimum (not just clipping and using that) is important because it makes the clip a one-sided safety net specifically against the ratio moving too far in the direction the advantage already favors -- it still allows the objective to discourage moves in the unfavorable direction without the clip's protection kicking in on the wrong side, which is a subtlety that a naive 'always clip the ratio' implementation gets wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer:
GAE is just an efficient way to blend low-bias, high-variance Monte Carlo returns with high-bias, low-variance one-step TD estimates, controlled by lambda -- and the trick is computing it backward through the trajectory in one pass by accumulating a running discounted sum of TD deltas, rather than recomputing multi-step returns from scratch for every timestep. Lambda close to 0 leans TD-like, lambda close to 1 leans Monte-Carlo-like.

For the PPO loss, the clipping is doing something specific that's easy to get wrong: you take the minimum of the plain importance-weighted advantage and a clipped-ratio version, not just always clip the ratio. That minimum is what makes the clip act as a one-sided safety net -- it caps how much credit you give an update that's moving the ratio too far in the favorable direction, but it still lets the loss discourage moves in the unfavorable direction without the clip getting in the way there. If you just hard-clip the ratio everywhere, you remove that asymmetry and the objective stops behaving the way PPO's actually designed to.
commonMistakes: Always clipping the ratio instead of taking the min of clipped and unclipped objectives, breaking PPO's intended asymmetry
Recomputing multi-step returns from scratch instead of using GAE's efficient backward recursion
Using the wrong sign convention, maximizing instead of minimizing the negative surrogate loss
Forgetting to detach old_logp (computed under the pre-update policy) before computing the ratio
keyPoints: GAE blends TD and Monte Carlo advantage estimates via lambda, computed efficiently backward through a trajectory
PPO's clipped objective takes the minimum of unclipped and clipped importance-weighted advantage
The min (not unconditional clipping) creates PPO's intended one-sided safety behavior
old_logp must come from the pre-update policy snapshot, detached from the current graph

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct GAE backward recursion
Correct PPO clipped objective using min(), not unconditional clip
Correct handling of old vs. new log-probabilities
Clean, runnable code

questions.title: Implementing the KL Penalty Term for RLHF Reward Shaping
questions.prompt: Implement the per-token KL penalty against a frozen reference policy and combine it with a reward-model score to produce the shaped reward used in an RLHF PPO update.
questions.modelAnswer:
The per-token KL estimate used in practice is the difference between the policy's and the reference model's log-probability of the actually-generated token at each position, which is an unbiased sample-based estimate of the KL divergence at that position (not the full-distribution KL over the vocabulary, which would require summing over every token, not just the sampled one) -- this sampled approximation is standard and computationally far cheaper. The reference model must run with gradients disabled and frozen weights, since it exists purely as a fixed comparison point, never updated during RL.

The shaped reward given to the RL algorithm at each generated token combines the sparse, sequence-level reward-model score (typically only awarded at the final token, with zero elsewhere) with this per-token KL penalty subtracted at every position, scaled by the KL coefficient beta: reward_per_token = kl_coef_scaled_penalty at every step, plus the reward-model score added only at the sequence's last token. This gives the PPO algorithm a dense per-token signal (the KL cost) layered under a sparse terminal signal (task reward), which is important because a purely terminal reward with no per-step shaping gives the advantage estimator very little to work with early in a long generation.

The reference model runs under no_grad with completely frozen weights the whole time; it's a fixed yardstick, never updated.

The shaped reward you actually feed PPO combines two things: the reward-model's score, which is sparse and typically only shows up at the very last token of the sequence, and this per-token KL penalty, scaled by beta, subtracted at every single position. That matters because a reward that's purely terminal gives the advantage estimator almost nothing to work with for most of a long generation -- the per-token KL cost gives PPO a dense signal layered under the sparse task reward, so early tokens aren't just getting zero credit assignment the whole way through.

def shaped_reward(rm_score, kl_per_token, kl_coef, seq_len):

    return reward

questions.title: Building a Custom Gymnasium Environment for Query-Plan Selection
questions.prompt: Implement a custom Gymnasium environment that frames database query-plan selection as an RL problem, with a reward based on execution cost relative to the database's own optimizer choice.
questions.modelAnswer:
The environment's observation needs to encode the features that actually distinguish which plan is cheap for a given query -- table/index statistics, predicate selectivity estimates, join cardinalities -- not the raw SQL text, since the RL agent is choosing among execution strategies, not generating SQL. The action space is a discrete choice among candidate plans the database's query planner can be hinted to use (via plan hints or forced join orders), and each episode is naturally a single step: pick a plan, execute it, observe the cost, done -- there's no multi-step sequential structure within one query's plan selection, which makes this a contextual bandit dressed as an RL environment more than a long-horizon MDP, and that's fine, it doesn't need to be forced into a longer episode structure it doesn't have.

The reward is defined relative to the database's own optimizer's cost estimate, not an absolute cost, specifically so the agent is rewarded for beating the existing optimizer rather than just being rewarded for cheap queries in general (which would make the reward scale wildly across queries of very different sizes). Execution needs a hard timeout, both to protect the research infrastructure from runaway queries and because a timeout itself is informative: a plan that's picked and times out is strong evidence that plan was a bad choice, and should be fed back as a strongly negative reward rather than silently dropped from the training data.

questions.title: Implementing DPO Loss From Scratch
questions.prompt: Implement the Direct Preference Optimization loss function from scratch, computing it from policy and reference log-probabilities on chosen/rejected response pairs.
questions.code:
def dpo_loss(policy_chosen_logp, policy_rejected_logp,
             ref_chosen_logp, ref_rejected_logp, beta=0.1):
    chosen_logratio = policy_chosen_logp - ref_chosen_logp
    rejected_logratio = policy_rejected_logp - ref_rejected_logp
    logits = beta * (chosen_logratio - rejected_logratio)
    loss = -F.logsigmoid(logits).mean()
    return loss
questions.modelAnswer:
DPO's loss is built from the log-ratio of policy to reference probability for the chosen and rejected response separately -- how much more (or less) likely the current policy makes each response relative to the frozen reference model -- and the training signal is the difference between those two log-ratios, scaled by beta, pushed through a logistic loss. Beta plays the same role as the KL coefficient in PPO-based RLHF: a larger beta more strongly discourages the policy from drifting from the reference model while still separating chosen from rejected, a smaller beta allows more aggressive separation at the cost of drifting further from the reference distribution.

Computing the log-probabilities correctly requires summing per-token log-probabilities over the full response (not averaging, since DPO's derivation is in terms of sequence-level probability, which is a product of token probabilities, i.e. sum of log-probabilities), and the reference log-probabilities must come from a frozen copy of the model evaluated with no gradients, typically computed once and cached before training since they don't change. A common correctness bug is averaging instead of summing token log-probabilities, which breaks the sequence-level probability interpretation the DPO loss derivation depends on.

questions.title: Implementing a Logit-Lens Probe on a Mid-Layer Residual Stream
questions.prompt: Implement a logit-lens probe: take the residual stream at an intermediate transformer layer and project it through the model's own final unembedding matrix to see what token it would predict if generation stopped there.
questions.modelAnswer:
The logit lens works on the premise that a transformer's final unembedding matrix (which is often tied to the token embedding matrix) can be applied to the residual stream at any layer, not just the final one, because the residual stream is a running sum that later layers only add to -- so an intermediate state is a meaningful partial prediction, even though the model never actually used that intermediate projection during real generation. Applying the model's final layer norm before unembedding is important for correctness, because later layers were trained assuming that normalization happens at the end, and skipping it produces logits on a different, uncalibrated scale that are harder to interpret.

The resulting early-layer predictions typically look much less confident and sometimes genuinely wrong relative to the final-layer output, and the pattern of how the top predicted token changes from layer to layer is itself the useful signal -- it shows roughly where in the network a correct final answer gets 'locked in,' which is a cheap, rough localization tool. The important caveat: the logit lens shows you what interpretation the final unembedding assigns to an intermediate state, not what the model is 'actually thinking' at that layer in any stronger sense, since later layers can and do read the residual stream in ways the final unembedding matrix doesn't capture.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The whole premise is that the residual stream is a running sum -- later layers only add to it, they don't replace it -- so you can take the final unembedding matrix, which the model normally only applies at the very end, and apply it early instead, and get a legitimate partial prediction out of an intermediate layer, even though the model itself never actually does that during real generation. I'd always apply the model's own final layer norm before unembedding, because later layers were trained assuming normalization happens right at the end, and skipping that step puts your early logits on an uncalibrated scale that's hard to read meaningfully.

What you get out of this is usually much less confident, sometimes just wrong, predictions early on, and the actual useful signal is watching how the top predicted token changes layer by layer -- that gives you a cheap, rough sense of where in the network the final answer gets locked in. The caveat I'd always attach: this shows you what the model's own final unembedding matrix thinks an intermediate state looks like, not some deeper truth about what the model is 'actually thinking' at that layer -- later layers can read that same residual stream in ways the final unembedding doesn't capture at all.

Treating early-layer logit-lens predictions as the model's 'true internal belief' rather than a projection artifact
Using an untied, separately-initialized unembedding matrix without checking it's actually the one the model uses
Not tracking how the top-predicted token changes across layers, missing the localization signal that makes the lens useful

questions.title: Implementing Activation Checkpointing for Memory Savings
questions.prompt: Implement activation (gradient) checkpointing for a transformer block to trade compute for memory during training, and explain what memory is actually saved and what the recomputation cost is.
questions.modelAnswer:
Normal backpropagation requires keeping every intermediate activation from the forward pass in memory so the backward pass has what it needs to compute gradients, and for a deep transformer this activation memory often dominates total training memory, especially at long sequence lengths. Activation checkpointing instead discards the intermediate activations inside a checkpointed block right after the forward pass computes its output, keeping only the block's input, and when the backward pass reaches that block, it reruns the forward computation on the saved input to regenerate the activations just-in-time before computing gradients.

The tradeoff is explicit: memory drops roughly in proportion to how much of the network's activations are checkpointed rather than retained, but each checkpointed block's forward pass runs twice (once during the original forward, once during the recomputation in backward), adding roughly the cost of one extra forward pass through the checkpointed portion of the network -- typically 20-30% wall-clock slowdown in practice, not the naive doubling it might sound like, since only the checkpointed segments are recomputed, not the whole network's non-tensor bookkeeping. Checkpointing every block maximizes memory savings at the largest compute cost; checkpointing only the largest or most memory-hungry blocks is a common middle ground when memory pressure doesn't require checkpointing everything.
questions.professionalAnswer:

Checkpointing changes the deal: instead of keeping a block's intermediate activations around, you throw them away right after the forward pass and just keep the block's input. When backward actually needs those activations, you rerun the forward computation on that saved input to regenerate them on the spot, right before computing gradients for that block.

The tradeoff is real and worth stating plainly: memory drops roughly in proportion to how much you checkpoint, but every checkpointed block's forward pass effectively runs twice -- once originally, once again during the recompute in backward. In practice that's usually something like a 20-30% wall-clock slowdown, not a flat doubling, since you're only re-running the checkpointed segments, not duplicating everything in the network. I'd usually checkpoint the biggest, most memory-hungry blocks first rather than reaching straight for 'checkpoint everything,' unless memory pressure is bad enough that you genuinely need the full savings.

Assuming the slowdown is always exactly 2x rather than a partial, segment-dependent overhead
Checkpointing every block by default instead of targeting the largest/most memory-hungry ones first
Not realizing recomputation happens automatically during backward, assuming it requires manually calling forward again

The tradeoff is reduced memory for roughly 20-30% extra wall-clock time, not a flat 2x

questions.title: Implementing Sequence Packing for a Pretraining Data Loader
questions.prompt: Implement sequence packing for a pretraining data loader: concatenate multiple variable-length documents into fixed-length training sequences while preventing attention across document boundaries.
questions.modelAnswer:
Padding every document out to a fixed sequence length wastes enormous compute on tokens that carry no training signal, especially when document length varies widely, so sequence packing instead concatenates many documents end to end (separated by an end-of-sequence token) into one long stream and slices that stream into fixed-length chunks, which keeps essentially every token in every training example meaningful and dramatically improves token-per-FLOP efficiency compared to padding-heavy batching.

The correctness-critical part that the naive concatenation above doesn't yet handle is attention masking: a standard causal attention mask allows a token to attend to everything before it in the sequence, which after packing would let a token from one document attend across the boundary into an unrelated, previous document -- a document-boundary-aware attention mask (or a reset of position ids at each document boundary) is required so each document only attends within itself, otherwise the model is trained on spurious cross-document context it will never see at inference time in that form. Many implementations track document boundaries alongside the packed token ids specifically to construct this block-diagonal attention mask at each boundary.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Padding every document out to the same fixed length wastes a huge amount of compute on tokens that carry zero training signal, especially once document lengths vary a lot. Packing instead concatenates a bunch of documents end-to-end, separated by an EOS token, into one long stream, and slices that stream into fixed-length chunks -- so almost every token in every training example is doing real work, which is a big efficiency win over padding-heavy batching.

The part that's easy to get wrong, and that the simple concatenation code doesn't handle on its own, is attention masking. A normal causal mask lets a token attend to everything before it in the sequence -- after packing, that would let a token in document B attend across the boundary into unrelated document A, which the model will never see in that form at actual inference time. You need a document-boundary-aware attention mask, or reset position ids at each boundary, so each document only attends within itself. I'd track document boundaries alongside the packed token ids specifically so I can build that block-diagonal mask correctly at training time, not bolt it on as an afterthought.
questions.example:
# tracking boundaries for masking
def pack_with_boundaries(documents, seq_len, eos_id):
    packed, boundaries, current, current_bounds = [], [], [], []
    pos = 0
    for doc in documents:
        tokens = doc + [eos_id]
        current += tokens
        current_bounds.append((pos, pos + len(tokens)))
        pos += len(tokens)
        while len(current) >= seq_len:
            packed.append(current[:seq_len])
            boundaries.append(current_bounds)
            current, current_bounds, pos = current[seq_len:], [], 0
    return packed, boundaries

Not resetting position ids at document boundaries when using absolute positional encoding
Truncating a document's final chunk without padding it, producing variable-length final batches that break fixed-shape assumptions
Treating packing purely as a data-loading convenience without accounting for the compute-efficiency reason it matters
keyPoints: Sequence packing concatenates documents to avoid wasting compute on padding tokens
A document-boundary-aware attention mask (or position-id reset) is required to prevent cross-document attention leakage
Tracking document boundaries alongside packed tokens is necessary to build that mask correctly
Packing substantially improves token-per-FLOP training efficiency versus padding-heavy batching

Identifies and addresses the cross-document attention leakage issue
Explains the compute-efficiency motivation correctly

questions.title: Implementing a LoRA Layer From Scratch
questions.prompt: Implement a LoRA linear layer from scratch: a frozen base weight matrix with a trainable low-rank update applied alongside it.
questions.modelAnswer:
The base layer's weights must have requires_grad explicitly disabled so the optimizer never updates them, leaving A and B as the only trainable parameters -- this is what makes LoRA cheap, since gradients and optimizer state are only needed for the small rank-r matrices, not the full weight matrix. B is initialized to zero (A is initialized small/random) specifically so that at the start of training the LoRA update contributes exactly zero, meaning the adapted model is numerically identical to the frozen base model before any training happens, rather than starting from a random perturbation that would need to be trained away first.

The alpha/rank scaling factor controls the effective magnitude of the low-rank update independent of the chosen rank, which matters because changing rank without compensating the scale would change how much influence the adapter has at a given learning rate, making rank and learning-rate tuning entangled if the scale weren't normalized this way. The forward pass computes the base layer's output and adds the low-rank update computed as x times A-transpose times B-transpose, scaled -- this ordering (down-project via A, then up-project via B) is what keeps the intermediate dimension at rank r rather than at the full feature dimension, which is the entire source of the parameter and compute savings.

questions.title: Implementing a Probing Classifier on Frozen Activations
questions.prompt: Implement a probing classifier that trains a small linear model on a frozen transformer's intermediate activations to test whether a specific concept is linearly represented at that layer, including the correct training discipline (frozen backbone, held-out evaluation).
questions.modelAnswer:
A probing classifier's validity depends entirely on the backbone staying completely frozen -- activations are extracted under no_grad with the backbone's weights untouched, and only the small probe (here a single linear layer) is trained, because the question being asked is specifically whether the concept is already linearly recoverable from the frozen representation, not whether a sufficiently large trained classifier could learn to extract it some other way. Using a highly expressive probe (a deep MLP, say) undermines the interpretability conclusion, since a powerful enough probe can learn to extract almost any concept from almost any representation given enough capacity, making the result say more about the probe than the model.

The other essential discipline is a proper held-out train/test split on the probing dataset itself, separate from whatever data the base model was trained or evaluated on, and reporting probe accuracy against a sensible baseline (majority-class accuracy, or probing a comparison layer/an untrained model) rather than in isolation -- a probe that gets 85% accuracy is meaningless without knowing whether a baseline would get 80% anyway. A well-run probing study also checks probe accuracy across multiple layers to see where, if anywhere, the concept becomes linearly separable, since that layer-wise pattern is often more informative than any single layer's number.

questions.title: Implementing a Self-Critique and Revision Loop (Constitutional-AI Style)
questions.prompt: Implement a self-critique and revision loop in the style of constitutional AI / RLAIF: a model critiques its own response against a stated principle and produces a revised response, which becomes training data.
questions.code:
def self_critique_and_revise(model, prompt, initial_response, principle, generate_fn):
    critique_prompt = (
        f"Principle: {principle}\n\nPrompt: {prompt}\nResponse: {initial_response}\n\n"
        f"Identify ways this response violates the principle above. Be specific."
    )
    critique = generate_fn(model, critique_prompt)
    revision_prompt = (
        f"Prompt: {prompt}\nOriginal response: {initial_response}\nCritique: {critique}\n\n"
        f"Rewrite the response to address the critique while still answering the prompt."
    )
    revised_response = generate_fn(model, revision_prompt)
    return critique, revised_response
questions.modelAnswer:
The loop uses the same model in two distinct roles sequentially: first prompted explicitly to critique its own prior output against a named principle, producing a critique that identifies specific violations rather than a vague judgment, then prompted again to produce a revision conditioned on both the original response and its own critique. The revised response -- not the critique, and not the original -- becomes the training target, typically used either as SFT data (training the model directly on its own revised outputs) or as the preferred side of a preference pair against the original response for a subsequent RLAIF/DPO-style step.

The quality of the whole pipeline depends heavily on the critique step actually surfacing real, specific issues rather than the model rubber-stamping its own output with a vague or overly agreeable critique, which is a documented failure mode (the model being insufficiently critical of itself). Explicitly prompting for specific violations tied to the stated principle, rather than an open-ended 'is this good?' critique, measurably improves critique quality, and running this over a diverse set of principles and prompts, then filtering out cases where the critique found nothing to flag versus cases with substantive revisions, produces a more useful training set than treating every generated triple as equally valuable.

Then I prompt it again, conditioned on both the original response and that critique, to produce an actual revision. The thing that becomes training data is the revised response, not the critique itself and not the original -- used either directly as SFT data on the model's own improved outputs, or as the preferred half of a preference pair against the original for a follow-up RLAIF/DPO step.

And I wouldn't treat every generated critique/revision pair as equally useful -- I'd filter out the cases where the critique found nothing substantive to flag, and keep the ones where a real, specific revision actually happened.

questions.title: Implementing a Reward-Hacking Detection Check for an RLVR Verifier
questions.prompt: Implement a consistency check that flags likely reward hacking in an RLVR training run: detecting when a policy's reward is climbing on the verifier while its outputs show signs of gaming the verifier rather than genuinely solving the task.
questions.code:
def reward_hacking_signals(completions, rewards, reference_eval_fn):
    verifier_reward_mean = float(np.mean(rewards))
    reference_scores = [reference_eval_fn(c) for c in completions]
    reference_mean = float(np.mean(reference_scores))
    gap = verifier_reward_mean - reference_mean
    short_circuit_rate = sum(1 for c in completions if len(c.split()) < 5) / len(completions)
    return {
        "verifier_reward_mean": verifier_reward_mean,
        "reference_eval_mean": reference_mean,
        "verifier_reference_gap": gap,
        "degenerate_short_output_rate": short_circuit_rate,
    }
questions.modelAnswer:
A single training metric (verifier reward climbing) cannot distinguish genuine improvement from exploitation of the verifier, so detecting reward hacking requires a second, independent signal that the policy cannot directly optimize against -- typically a held-out reference evaluation (a different, stricter verifier, a human spot-check sample, or a stronger model's judgment) run periodically on the same completions the training verifier scored. A growing gap between the training verifier's reward and this independent reference score, especially if the verifier reward keeps climbing while the reference score plateaus or drops, is the core quantitative signature of reward hacking in progress.

Beyond the aggregate gap metric, specific degenerate-output heuristics catch common hacking patterns directly: unusually short or templated outputs that happen to satisfy a loose verifier pattern without real content, repeated exact-duplicate completions across different prompts, or outputs that pass the verifier's specific check (e.g. exact string match) while failing an obviously-related but differently-phrased check. None of these heuristics alone is proof of hacking, but tracking them over the course of training and flagging when several move together (rising verifier reward, rising verifier-reference gap, rising degenerate-output rate) gives a research engineer an early warning well before the problem is severe enough to show up in a final held-out eval.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The training verifier's own reward number can't tell you whether you're looking at genuine improvement or exploitation, because by definition the policy is optimizing against exactly that number. What catches it is a second, independent signal the policy isn't directly optimizing -- a held-out reference evaluation, a stricter verifier, a human spot-check, or a stronger model's judgment -- run periodically on the same completions the training verifier already scored. The thing I actually watch is the gap between the two: if the verifier reward keeps climbing while that independent reference score plateaus or drops, that gap widening is the core signature of reward hacking in progress.

On top of that gap metric, I'd add a few concrete degenerate-output heuristics, because they catch specific, common hacking patterns directly: unusually short or templated outputs that happen to satisfy a loose verifier pattern with no real content behind them, exact-duplicate completions showing up across unrelated prompts, or outputs that pass the verifier's specific check but clearly fail an obviously related check phrased slightly differently. No single one of these proves hacking is happening, but when several of them start moving together -- verifier reward up, verifier-reference gap widening, degenerate-output rate climbing -- that's an early warning worth acting on well before it shows up as a real problem in a final held-out eval.

Treating a single degenerate-output heuristic as definitive proof of reward hacking rather than one signal among several
Running the independent reference evaluation too rarely to catch a hacking trend before it's severe
Not checking for exact-duplicate or templated outputs, missing a common and easy-to-detect hacking pattern

A widening gap between verifier reward and reference evaluation is the core quantitative signature
Degenerate-output heuristics (short/templated/duplicate completions) catch specific common hacking patterns

questions.title: Pretraining Run Regressed Silently After a Data-Mixture Change
questions.prompt: A pretraining run's training loss curve looks completely normal after a data-mixture rebalancing was deployed mid-run, but a downstream code-generation eval that ran weekly shows a sharp drop two weeks later. Walk through how you'd diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer:
A normal training loss curve after a mixture change is expected and uninformative here, because training loss is dominated by the new mixture's own distribution -- if the rebalancing reduced the code domain's weight, the model can get smoothly better at predicting the new (code-reduced) mixture while getting measurably worse at the specific downstream skill that mixture no longer emphasizes, and the aggregate loss number has no way to surface that domain-specific regression. The first step is confirming the timeline: pin down exactly which training step the mixture change took effect at, and check whether the code eval's two-week-later drop lines up with roughly that many steps of reduced code exposure, not a coincidental unrelated event.

The second step is checking the mixture change itself for what actually happened versus what was intended -- a common real-world cause is the new mixture's code domain weight being lower than planned due to a config or sampling-weight bug, not a deliberate large intentional reduction, so comparing the realized sampled token counts per domain against the intended target ratios is essential, not just reading the config file. The third step is running a smaller, faster eval on an earlier checkpoint saved right at the mixture-change boundary to confirm the regression wasn't already present before the change (ruling out an unrelated cause), and a checkpoint from partway through the two weeks after to see if the regression developed gradually or suddenly, which further narrows the likely mechanism.

If the realized mixture weight is confirmed lower than intended, the fix is correcting the sampling configuration and deciding whether to continue training with the corrected mixture (accepting the already-elapsed regression) or restart from the pre-change checkpoint, which is itself a cost-benefit judgment based on how much compute would be lost either way.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't expect the training loss curve to show anything here, and that's not actually a mystery -- loss is dominated by the new mixture's own distribution. If code's weight went down, the model can get smoothly better at predicting the new mixture while getting worse at a specific downstream skill that mixture no longer emphasizes, and an aggregate loss number has no way to show that. First thing I'd pin down is the exact step the mixture change took effect, and check whether the eval's drop two weeks later lines up with roughly that many steps of reduced code exposure, rather than assuming it's related just because the timing is suspicious.

Then I'd go check what the mixture change actually did versus what was intended -- in my experience, this is very often a config or sampling-weight bug making the realized code ratio lower than whoever wrote the change thought it was, not a deliberate aggressive cut. I'd compare actual sampled token counts per domain against the target ratios, not just read the config file and assume it matches. I'd also pull an earlier checkpoint right at the change boundary and a checkpoint partway through the two weeks after, and run the eval on both, to confirm the regression wasn't already there before the change and to see whether it developed gradually or all at once -- that tells me a lot about the mechanism.

If it turns out the realized mixture really was off from the intended target, the fix is correcting the sampling config, and then it's a real cost-benefit call whether to keep training with the corrected mixture and accept the regression that already happened, or restart from before the change -- not an automatic 'always restart' decision.
commonMistakes: Treating a normal training loss curve as evidence the mixture change is unrelated to the eval regression
Not comparing realized sampled token counts per domain against the intended target ratios
Skipping checkpoints from the change boundary and the regression period, missing evidence about timing and mechanism
Jumping straight to restarting the run without first confirming the actual cause
