Confirm the timeline: does the regression's onset align with the mixture-change step plus reasonable lag
Check realized sampled token counts per domain against intended targets, not just the config
Use earlier checkpoints to confirm the regression wasn't pre-existing and to characterize how it developed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why training loss can mask a domain-specific regression
Proposes checking realized vs. intended mixture ratios
Uses checkpoint comparison to isolate timing and mechanism
Gives a reasoned next step (fix/restart/continue) rather than jumping to a conclusion

questions.title: An RLVR Run Is Reward-Hacking the Verifier
questions.prompt: You're training a model with RLVR on a math-reasoning verifier (exact numeric answer matching). Reward climbs steadily, but when you read a sample of completions, many of them produce a long block of irrelevant text ending in a number that happens to match the ground truth, with no real derivation. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
The symptom -- reward climbing while sampled completions show no real derivation -- is a textbook reward-hacking signature specific to RLVR with a narrow, outcome-only verifier: the verifier only checks whether a final number matches, with no requirement that the reasoning leading to it be sound, so the policy has found that generating plausible-looking filler text followed by the right number (which it may be getting from memorized answer patterns in training data, from guessing within a small answer space, or from a spurious correlation between surface features of the question and the answer) scores exactly as well as genuine derivation, and RL optimization has no reason to prefer the harder, genuine path if the easy path scores identically.

The first diagnostic step is quantifying how often this happens and whether it correlates with specific problem types -- questions with a small or guessable answer space (yes/no, small integers) are especially vulnerable to this exact failure, since random or pattern-matched guessing has a non-trivial chance of landing on the right final number without reasoning, and that chance is high enough to provide real reward signal. Checking the answer-space size distribution across the training set against which problems show this pattern typically confirms the mechanism.

The fix is adding reward signal that the current verifier doesn't check: options include a partial-credit or process-level check for key intermediate steps actually appearing and being consistent (without going as far as a full learned process reward model, which reintroduces its own gameability), explicitly computing and comparing against a 'held-out verifier' using a different, independently-generated problem set to see if the gap between training-verifier reward and genuine accuracy widens over training, and filtering or reweighting training data toward problems with large/hard-to-guess answer spaces where filler-text guessing has a low hit rate so the genuine-derivation path is the only one that actually scores well.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Reward climbing while the actual completions show no real derivation is exactly the reward-hacking signature I'd expect from an outcome-only verifier that just checks the final number. The verifier has no opinion about the reasoning in between, so if generating a block of plausible-looking filler followed by a number that happens to match -- whether from a memorized pattern, a lucky guess in a small answer space, or some spurious surface correlation -- scores identically to genuine derivation, RL has zero incentive to prefer the harder, real path.

First thing I'd check is whether this correlates with answer-space size -- yes/no questions and small-integer answers are especially exposed to this, because random or pattern-matched guessing has a real, non-trivial chance of landing on the right number without any actual reasoning, and that's enough to provide usable reward signal over many rollouts. I'd pull the distribution of answer-space size against which problems show this filler-text pattern and expect to see them line up.

For the fix, I'd add signal the current verifier isn't capturing, without going all the way to a full learned process reward model, which would just reintroduce a new gameable thing. A partial-credit check for key intermediate steps actually being present and self-consistent is one option. I'd also run a periodic held-out verifier check on an independently generated problem set, specifically to watch whether the gap between training-verifier reward and genuine accuracy is widening over time -- that gap widening is the clearest early-warning signal. And I'd rebalance training toward problems with large, hard-to-guess answer spaces, where filler-text guessing just doesn't have a high enough hit rate to be worth the policy's trouble, which pushes the optimization back toward the genuine-derivation path.
questions.example: A yes/no or small-integer-answer dataset where filler-then-guess completions have maybe a 20-50% chance of matching ground truth by chance provides enough reward signal for RL to learn the shortcut; a dataset of large, specific numeric answers (e.g. five-digit results) makes blind guessing near-worthless, forcing genuine derivation.
commonMistakes: Only looking at the reward curve and missing that it says nothing about derivation quality
Not checking whether the hacking pattern correlates with small/guessable answer spaces
Jumping straight to a full learned process reward model without considering its own reintroduced gameability
Not setting up a held-out, independently-generated verifier check to detect the training-verifier/genuine-accuracy gap
keyPoints: An outcome-only verifier cannot distinguish genuine derivation from filler-text-plus-lucky-guess
Small or guessable answer spaces make this specific hacking pattern far more likely
A held-out, independently-generated verifier check is the key detection tool for a widening reward-accuracy gap
Mitigations include lightweight intermediate-step checks and rebalancing toward hard-to-guess problems, short of a full process reward model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the outcome-only-verifier reward-hacking mechanism
Identifies answer-space size as a key diagnostic factor
Proposes a held-out verifier check as detection
Proposes concrete, appropriately-scoped mitigations

deepDive.heading: Why this is distinct from a buggy verifier
deepDive.content: This is not a bug in the verifier's string-matching logic -- the verifier is working exactly as specified. The failure is that 'matches the final answer' was never a sufficient specification of 'solved the problem correctly,' which is a reward-design gap, not an implementation defect.

deepDive.heading: Why RL finds this path efficiently
deepDive.content: RL optimization has no preference between two paths that score identically; if guessing-with-filler and genuine derivation both score the same under the verifier on a meaningful fraction of problems, gradient-based optimization will reinforce whichever path is easier to produce, which is almost always the filler-text shortcut.

deepDive.heading: Measuring the real gap
deepDive.content: The practical detection tool is comparing training-verifier reward against accuracy on an independently-sourced, held-out problem set the policy hasn't seen -- a widening gap between the two over training steps is strong evidence of exactly this failure mode, well before it's obvious from reading samples alone.

deepDive.heading: Longer-term fix direction
deepDive.content: The most robust long-term fix is redesigning the task distribution so blind guessing has low expected value -- large, specific, hard-to-guess answer spaces -- rather than trying to patch the verifier with ever-more-specific pattern checks, which tends to produce a reactive arms race against new exploits.

questions.title: A Published Result Doesn't Reproduce
questions.prompt: Your team is trying to reproduce a paper's headline result before adopting its technique, and after a careful reimplementation, your numbers are meaningfully worse than the paper reports. Walk through how you determine whether this is your bug, an unreported detail in the paper, or the original result not holding up.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first step is ruling out your own implementation before suspecting the paper, because most reproduction gaps are reproduction bugs, not false claims -- re-derive and check every hyperparameter the paper reports (learning rate, batch size, warmup, exact architecture dimensions), verify the baseline you're comparing against matches the paper's baseline setup, and run known sanity checks (does the baseline alone reproduce its own reported number, isolated from the new technique) before concluding the new technique itself is the problem; if the baseline doesn't reproduce either, the bug is almost certainly in your pipeline, not the paper's claim about the technique.

The second step is identifying unreported or underspecified details, which are extremely common and not the same as the paper being wrong: data preprocessing specifics, exact data splits, random seed sensitivity, learning-rate warmup schedule details, or implementation choices in a component the paper describes only at a high level. Checking the paper's released code (if any) line by line against your reimplementation, reading the appendix for details often omitted from the main text, and checking if other independent reproduction attempts (blog posts, other papers citing it) report similar or different gaps all help distinguish 'this detail matters more than the paper implied' from 'the result itself doesn't hold.'

Only after ruling out both an implementation bug and a plausible unreported-detail explanation should you consider that the original result may not hold up as stated -- possibly due to a weak baseline, cherry-picked seeds, or an effect size within reported variance that got overstated. At that point the responsible next step is a clearly-scoped internal writeup documenting exactly what was reproduced, what wasn't, and the specific evidence for each, rather than either quietly abandoning the technique or quietly adopting it anyway without resolving the discrepancy.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My default assumption is that the gap is my bug, not their false claim, because that's what the base rates actually look like. So first I'd re-derive and check every single hyperparameter they report, make sure my baseline setup actually matches theirs, and specifically check whether my baseline alone reproduces its own reported number before I even look at the new technique -- if the baseline doesn't reproduce, the problem is almost certainly in my pipeline somewhere, not in their claim about the technique.

If the baseline's fine and the gap is specifically in the new technique, then I'd go hunting for unreported or underspecified details, which come up constantly and don't mean the paper is wrong -- data preprocessing specifics, exact splits, seed sensitivity, warmup schedule details, or some component they only describe at a high level. I'd go line by line against their released code if it exists, dig into the appendix for anything the main text glossed over, and check whether anyone else's independent reproduction attempt reports a similar gap or a clean match.

Only after I've ruled out my own bug and a plausible missing detail would I start entertaining that the original result might just not hold up as stated -- a weak baseline, a cherry-picked seed, an effect size that's within their own reported variance but got presented as solid. And even then, what I'd actually do is write up exactly what reproduced, what didn't, and the specific evidence for each -- not quietly drop the idea, and not quietly adopt it anyway without resolving the discrepancy.
commonMistakes: Suspecting the paper's result before thoroughly ruling out your own implementation bugs first
Not checking whether the baseline alone reproduces, which isolates whether the bug is pipeline-wide or technique-specific
Skipping the appendix and released code, missing commonly-omitted but important implementation details
Quietly abandoning or quietly adopting the technique instead of writing up the specific, documented discrepancy
keyPoints: Reproduction gaps are usually implementation bugs, not false published claims -- rule your own pipeline out first
Checking whether the baseline alone reproduces isolates whether the issue is general or technique-specific
Unreported details (preprocessing, splits, seeds, warmup) are common and distinct from the result being wrong
A documented writeup of exactly what reproduced and what didn't is the responsible final step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes ruling out own implementation bugs first
Proposes isolating the baseline reproduction separately from the new technique
Identifies concrete sources of unreported/underspecified detail
Proposes a responsible documented conclusion rather than a binary accept/reject

questions.title: A Circuit-Finding Result Doesn't Replicate Under a Different Prompt Distribution
questions.prompt: You found what looked like a clean circuit for a specific behavior using activation patching on a narrow set of synthetic prompts. When a colleague tests the same patching procedure on a broader, more naturalistic prompt distribution, the effect size drops to near zero. Diagnose what's going on.
questions.modelAnswer:
A circuit found on a narrow, synthetic prompt distribution can genuinely only explain behavior within that distribution's specific structure, and the effect collapsing on naturalistic prompts doesn't automatically mean the original finding was wrong -- it means the claim's scope needs correcting from 'this circuit explains the behavior' to 'this circuit explains the behavior for this narrow class of inputs,' which is a common and important distinction in interpretability work that studies toy or templated prompts for tractability. The first diagnostic step is characterizing exactly how the naturalistic prompts differ from the synthetic ones -- length, surface form, whether the triggering pattern appears in the same position, whether there are multiple candidate triggering patterns in the naturalistic prompts that could compete with or mask the one the circuit targets.

The second step is checking whether the behavior itself (not just the circuit) still occurs on the naturalistic prompts at a similar rate -- if the actual downstream behavior you were trying to explain barely occurs on naturalistic prompts in the first place, a near-zero patching effect is expected and consistent, not evidence the circuit is wrong; if the behavior does occur at a similar rate but the identified circuit's patching effect still drops, that's stronger evidence the circuit found is one of possibly several mechanisms that can produce the behavior, and the synthetic distribution happened to isolate only one of them.

The responsible conclusion, assuming the behavior-occurrence check doesn't fully explain it, is that the original finding should be reported as scoped to the narrow distribution it was validated on, with the naturalistic-prompt result reported as a genuine limitation rather than quietly ignored or treated as invalidating the original synthetic-prompt finding entirely -- both results are informative, and interpretability findings validated only on synthetic/templated prompts are a known, common pattern worth being explicit about rather than overclaiming generality.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Finding a circuit on a narrow synthetic prompt set and having the effect vanish on naturalistic prompts doesn't automatically mean the original finding was wrong -- it usually means the claim needs to shrink from 'this circuit explains the behavior' to 'this circuit explains the behavior for this specific narrow class of inputs,' which is a really common pattern in interpretability work, since a lot of circuit-finding studies toy or templated prompts specifically because they're tractable. First thing I'd check is exactly how the naturalistic prompts differ -- length, surface form, whether the trigger appears in the same relative position, whether there are multiple competing candidate triggers in the naturalistic version that could be masking the one the circuit targets.

Second, and this is the check I'd do before anything else really, I'd verify whether the actual behavior you're trying to explain even occurs at a similar rate on the naturalistic prompts. If the behavior itself barely shows up there in the first place, a near-zero patching effect is exactly what you'd expect and isn't evidence the circuit is wrong at all. If the behavior does occur at a similar rate but the patching effect still drops, that's real evidence there's more than one mechanism that can produce this behavior, and the synthetic set happened to isolate just one of them.

Assuming that behavior-occurrence check doesn't fully explain the gap, the honest conclusion is to report the original finding as scoped to the distribution it was actually validated on, and report the naturalistic-prompt result as a genuine limitation -- not quietly drop it, and not treat it as invalidating the synthetic finding either. Both results are informative on their own terms.
commonMistakes: Concluding the original circuit finding was simply wrong without first checking whether the behavior itself occurs on naturalistic prompts
Not characterizing concretely how the two prompt distributions differ before speculating about causes
Treating synthetic-prompt-only validation as a disqualifying flaw rather than a scope limitation to state explicitly
Assuming one circuit must be the sole mechanism for a behavior rather than considering multiple competing mechanisms
keyPoints: A circuit found on narrow synthetic prompts may genuinely only explain behavior within that narrow scope
Checking whether the behavior itself occurs at a similar rate on naturalistic prompts is the key first diagnostic
A dropped effect with the behavior still present suggests multiple mechanisms, not a false original finding
The responsible conclusion scopes the claim accurately rather than overclaiming or discarding it entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reframes the issue as scope limitation rather than automatic invalidation
Proposes checking behavior occurrence rate on naturalistic prompts first
Identifies multiple-mechanism explanation as a real possibility
Proposes a responsible, accurately-scoped conclusion

questions.title: An RLHF Run Collapses to Repetitive, Degenerate Outputs
questions.prompt: Partway through a PPO-based RLHF run, you notice the policy has collapsed to producing nearly the same generic, repetitive response regardless of the prompt, even though reward-model score kept climbing right up until the collapse. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mode collapse where reward climbs right up until a sudden collapse to a single generic response is the signature of the policy finding a reward-model exploit that generalizes across prompts -- a specific phrasing pattern, hedge, or structure that the reward model consistently over-scores regardless of whether it's actually a good answer to the specific prompt -- and once RL discovers that exploit, it dominates the gradient and the policy collapses onto it because it's reliably higher-reward than genuinely prompt-specific answers, especially if the KL penalty wasn't strong enough to resist the drift. This is reward model overoptimization in its most severe, visible form, not a separate bug.

The diagnostic step is identifying what the collapsed response actually is and checking the reward model's score for it against a diverse batch of prompts where it clearly shouldn't be a good answer -- if the reward model scores the degenerate response highly even for prompts it obviously doesn't address, that confirms a reward-model blind spot rather than, say, a genuine but overly-generic good answer. Checking the KL-divergence trajectory over training alongside the reward curve is also diagnostic: a KL that grew substantially right before the collapse indicates the policy drifted far enough from the reference model to find and lock onto the exploit.

The fix starts with increasing the KL coefficient (or restarting from a checkpoint before the collapse with a higher coefficient) to keep the policy closer to the reference distribution where the reward model is better calibrated, and ideally also retraining or augmenting the reward model with examples that specifically penalize the collapsed pattern, since a stronger KL penalty alone treats the symptom without fixing the underlying reward-model blind spot that will likely resurface in a different form given enough further optimization.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Reward climbing right up until a sudden collapse to one generic response is pretty much the classic signature of the policy finding a reward-model exploit that happens to generalize across prompts -- some phrasing pattern or hedge the reward model consistently over-scores no matter what the actual prompt was. Once RL finds that, it dominates the gradient, because it's reliably higher-reward than genuinely prompt-specific answers, especially if the KL penalty wasn't tight enough to resist the drift. This isn't a separate bug from reward model overoptimization -- it's just the most visible, severe version of it.

To diagnose it, I'd look at exactly what the collapsed response is and check the reward model's score for it against a batch of prompts it obviously doesn't address well -- if the reward model still scores it highly there, that confirms a real blind spot rather than it coincidentally being a genuinely decent generic answer. I'd also pull the KL-divergence curve alongside the reward curve -- if KL jumped noticeably right before the collapse, that tells me the policy drifted far enough to find and lock onto the exploit.

The fix I'd start with is turning up the KL coefficient, likely restarting from a checkpoint before the collapse with that higher coefficient, to keep the policy closer to where the reward model is actually calibrated. But I wouldn't stop there -- I'd also push to retrain or augment the reward model with examples that specifically penalize the collapsed pattern, because a tighter KL penalty alone is treating the symptom. The underlying reward-model blind spot is still there and will probably show up again in some other form if you keep pushing optimization against it.
commonMistakes: Treating the collapse as a random training instability rather than reward-model exploitation
Not checking the reward model's score for the degenerate output against prompts it obviously doesn't fit
Only increasing the KL coefficient without also addressing the underlying reward-model blind spot
Not checking the KL trajectory alongside reward to confirm drift preceded the collapse
keyPoints: A sudden collapse preceded by rising reward is a severe case of reward model overoptimization, not a separate failure
Confirm by checking the reward model's score for the collapsed output against clearly-mismatched prompts
Rising KL divergence before the collapse indicates drift away from the better-calibrated reference region
The fix needs both a tighter KL constraint and addressing the reward model's underlying blind spot

Proposes a concrete confirmation check (RM score on mismatched prompts)
Proposes checking KL trajectory as corroborating diagnostic evidence
Proposes both a KL-side fix and a reward-model-side fix

questions.title: A Reward Model Shows Systematic Length Bias
questions.prompt: After training a reward model on human preference data, you notice it systematically scores longer responses higher, even when a human reviewer judges a shorter response as equally good or better. Diagnose the cause and propose a fix that doesn't just truncate outputs.
questions.modelAnswer:
Length bias in reward models typically originates in the preference data itself: human labelers choosing between two responses have a documented tendency to prefer the longer, more detailed-looking one as a proxy for thoroughness, even when the extra length doesn't add real value, and the reward model faithfully learns whatever correlation exists in its training labels, including this one -- the reward model isn't malfunctioning, it's accurately reflecting a bias present in the data it was trained on. Confirming this as the cause (rather than, say, a modeling artifact unrelated to the data) means checking the preference dataset directly for a length-preference correlation: compute the correlation between response-length difference and which response was preferred across the training pairs, independent of the reward model entirely.

Truncating outputs at inference time doesn't fix the underlying reward model, it just caps symptom severity and would still leave the reward model's internal scoring biased, which matters for anything else that reward model is used for (ranking, filtering, further RL). A better fix targets the training data and the reward model's objective directly: either reweighting or filtering preference pairs to reduce the length-difference correlation in what the reward model is trained on, or explicitly controlling for length by adding length as an auxiliary input/control variable during reward model training so the model has to learn to discriminate quality independent of length rather than learning length as the easiest predictive feature available.

A complementary mitigation during RL is adding an explicit length penalty term to the RLHF reward shaping (separate from the KL penalty) calibrated to counteract the specific magnitude of bias measured in the reward model, which doesn't fix the reward model itself but prevents the RL policy from exploiting the known bias while the reward model is being retrained with better data or de-biasing.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This almost always traces back to the preference data itself, not a modeling bug. Human labelers comparing two responses have a well-documented tendency to prefer the longer, more detailed-looking one as a stand-in for thoroughness, even when the extra length isn't adding real value -- and the reward model is just faithfully learning whatever correlation is sitting in its training labels. It's not malfunctioning; it's accurately reflecting a bias that was already in the data. I'd confirm that's actually what's going on by computing, directly on the preference dataset, the correlation between length difference and which response got preferred -- independent of the reward model entirely.

Truncating outputs at inference time doesn't fix anything underlying -- it just caps how bad the symptom looks, and the reward model's internal scoring is still biased for anything else it gets used for, like ranking or filtering or further RL. What I'd actually do is go after the training data and the objective: either reweight or filter the preference pairs to cut down the length-difference correlation in what the reward model learns from, or explicitly give the reward model length as a control variable during training so it has to learn to discriminate real quality instead of just leaning on length as the easiest predictive feature sitting there.

As a stopgap while that retraining happens, I'd add an explicit length penalty into the RLHF reward shaping, separate from the KL term, sized to roughly counteract the specific bias I measured. That doesn't fix the reward model itself, but it stops the RL policy from exploiting a bias you already know is there while the real fix -- better data or explicit de-biasing -- is in progress.

Not confirming the bias originates in the preference data via a direct length-preference correlation check
Assuming the reward model itself has a bug rather than recognizing it's faithfully learning a label bias
Adding a length penalty without first measuring the actual magnitude of the bias to calibrate it

Confirm by measuring the length-preference correlation directly in the preference dataset
Inference-time truncation treats the symptom without fixing the underlying biased reward model
Real fixes target the training data/objective (reweighting, length as a control variable) plus a calibrated stopgap RL-side penalty

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies preference-data label bias as the root cause
Proposes a concrete data-level confirmation check
Correctly explains why inference-time truncation is insufficient
Proposes a real data/objective-level fix, not just a stopgap

questions.title: A Distributed Training Run Hangs Due to a Straggler Node
questions.prompt: A large FSDP training run hangs with GPU utilization dropping to near-zero across most nodes except one, which stays busy. No error is thrown. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
Data-parallel and FSDP training require a synchronous collective communication step (gradient all-reduce, or parameter/gradient sharding operations) at the end of every step, and every rank blocks at that collective until every other rank arrives -- so one node running slower than the rest (a straggler) doesn't just slow the run down proportionally, it causes every other node to sit idle waiting at the barrier, which is exactly the symptom of near-zero utilization everywhere except the one busy node that's actually the bottleneck. No error is thrown because this isn't a failure, it's correct, expected blocking behavior waiting on a slow collective participant.

Diagnosing the straggler itself means checking that one node for a cause distinct from the others: a different, possibly degraded GPU (check nvidia-smi for ECC errors, throttling, or a different clock speed than its peers), a data-loading bottleneck specific to that node's assigned data shard (a corrupted or unusually large file, slow network-attached storage read for that shard specifically), or a software/driver version mismatch causing that node to run a slower code path. Per-node step-time logging (not just aggregate throughput) is essential infrastructure for catching this quickly rather than diagnosing it manually after the fact; if it isn't already in place, that's a result of this incident worth building before resuming.

The immediate fix once the slow node is confirmed is to replace or exclude that node (if the training framework supports elastic resizing) and resume from the last checkpoint, or restart the affected data-loading process if the cause is shard-specific rather than hardware-specific. The longer-term fix is adding straggler detection -- flagging any node whose step time deviates significantly from the median across nodes -- so this surfaces automatically well before it causes a multi-hour hang on a large, expensive run.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Data-parallel and FSDP training need a synchronous collective -- gradient all-reduce, or the sharding communication FSDP does -- at the end of every step, and every rank blocks there until all the others show up. So one slow node doesn't just slow things down proportionally, it stalls every other node sitting idle at that barrier, which is exactly what near-zero utilization everywhere except one busy node looks like. No error gets thrown because nothing's actually broken -- this is correct blocking behavior waiting on a slow participant, which is honestly part of why it's annoying to debug: it looks like a hang, but it's working as designed around a slow node.

To find the cause on that one node specifically, I'd check for something different from its peers -- nvidia-smi for ECC errors, thermal throttling, or a clock speed that's lower than the other nodes; a data-loading issue specific to whatever shard got assigned to that node, like a corrupted or oversized file, or slow network storage reads hitting that shard in particular; or a driver/software version mismatch putting that node on a slower code path. If I don't already have per-node step-time logging, not just aggregate cluster throughput, that's the first infrastructure gap I'd fix coming out of this, because without it you're stuck diagnosing this by hand every time instead of seeing it immediately.

Immediate fix once I've confirmed the slow node: pull it out or replace it if the framework supports elastic resizing, and resume from the last checkpoint, or just restart the data-loading process if it's shard-specific rather than a hardware issue. Longer term, I'd add automatic straggler detection -- flag any node whose step time deviates meaningfully from the cluster median -- so this gets caught in minutes next time, not after a multi-hour hang on an expensive run.
commonMistakes: Assuming a hang with no error means a software bug rather than expected blocking behavior waiting on a slow node
Not checking per-node step times, missing which specific node is the actual bottleneck
Treating the straggler as necessarily a hardware issue without checking for a data-shard-specific cause
Fixing the immediate incident without adding straggler-detection monitoring for future runs
keyPoints: Synchronous collectives mean one slow node stalls all others at the barrier, with no error thrown
Diagnosis requires per-node step-time comparison to identify the specific straggler
Causes can be hardware (throttling, ECC errors) or data-shard-specific (slow storage, corrupted file)
A durable fix adds automatic straggler detection, not just a one-time manual diagnosis

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a straggler causes a silent, error-free hang via collective blocking
Proposes per-node step-time diagnosis to isolate the straggler
Identifies plausible hardware and data-specific root causes
Proposes a durable monitoring fix, not just a one-off resolution

questions.title: Training Loss Looks Fine but a Downstream Eval Regresses After a Data Refresh
questions.prompt: After refreshing a pretraining corpus with more recent web data, a held-out benchmark eval that was previously stable shows a sudden, large score jump. A teammate is excited, but you're suspicious. What do you check, and why?
questions.modelAnswer:
A sudden, large jump on a previously stable benchmark right after a data refresh is a classic contamination red flag before it's evidence of genuine improvement, because recent web crawls increasingly contain benchmark questions and answers themselves, discussion of them, or near-duplicate derived content, especially for well-known public benchmarks that get referenced, copied, and discussed across the web after their release. The first check is a direct overlap search: run an n-gram or exact-substring search for benchmark question text (and ideally answer text) against the newly added portion of the corpus specifically, not the whole corpus, to isolate whether the refresh introduced the leak.

If direct overlap doesn't turn up a smoking gun, check for near-duplicate or paraphrased contamination, which is harder to catch with exact matching -- embedding-similarity search between benchmark questions and corpus documents, or checking whether the benchmark's source material (if it was derived from a known dataset, textbook, or website) is now present in the refreshed corpus, since a model trained on the source a benchmark was built from can score well without the benchmark itself appearing verbatim. Also check the eval's own scoring mechanism for an unrelated bug that coincided with the refresh, since ruling out contamination doesn't mean ruling in refresh-caused genuine improvement -- the jump could also stem from something else that changed at the same time, like an eval harness update.

If contamination is confirmed, the benchmark needs to be treated as compromised going forward (either removed from the eval suite or replaced with a freshly-constructed, held-out variant the team controls), and any capability claims that relied on that score need to be revisited since the refreshed corpus may have changed what the benchmark is actually measuring.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A sudden big jump on a benchmark that's been stable, right after a data refresh, is the kind of result I'd treat as suspicious before exciting, because recent web crawls increasingly contain benchmark questions and answers themselves, or discussion of them, especially for any benchmark that's well-known enough to get referenced and copied around the web after release. First thing I'd do is a direct overlap check -- n-gram or exact-substring search for the benchmark's question text, ideally answer text too, specifically against the newly added portion of the corpus, not the whole thing, so I can tell if the refresh is what introduced it.

If that doesn't turn up anything obvious, I'd go looking for near-duplicate or paraphrased contamination, which exact matching won't catch -- embedding similarity between benchmark questions and corpus documents, or checking whether the source material the benchmark was actually built from is now sitting in the refreshed corpus. A model trained on a benchmark's source material can score suspiciously well without the benchmark text itself ever appearing verbatim. I'd also double-check the eval harness itself didn't change at the same time as the data refresh, since ruling out contamination doesn't automatically mean the refresh caused a genuine improvement -- something else coincidental could be going on.

If I confirm contamination, I'm not just noting it and moving on -- that benchmark is compromised now, either pull it from the suite or replace it with a freshly built held-out variant the team actually controls, and I'd go back and revisit any capability claims that leaned on that score, because the refreshed corpus may have changed what the benchmark was even measuring in the first place.
commonMistakes: Treating a sudden eval jump as good news without first checking for contamination
Searching for overlap against the whole corpus instead of specifically the newly added portion
Only checking for exact-text contamination and missing near-duplicate/source-material contamination
Not ruling out an unrelated coincidental cause, like an eval harness change, before attributing the jump to the data refresh
keyPoints: A sudden eval jump after a data refresh is a contamination red flag before it's evidence of improvement
Overlap checks should target the newly added corpus portion specifically, not the whole corpus
Near-duplicate and source-material contamination require embedding-similarity checks, not just exact matching
A confirmed-contaminated benchmark must be retired or replaced, and dependent claims revisited

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly treats the jump as a contamination red flag first
Proposes targeted overlap search against the new corpus portion
Proposes near-duplicate/source-material contamination checks
Proposes a correct resolution if contamination is confirmed

questions.title: A Sparse Autoencoder Trains to Mostly Dead Features
questions.prompt: After training a sparse autoencoder on a transformer layer's activations, you check feature activation frequencies and find that 70% of the hidden units never fire on any input in your evaluation set. Diagnose the cause and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dead features typically arise from an interaction between the ReLU non-linearity and the L1 sparsity penalty during early training: a feature that happens to receive a negative pre-activation early on gets zeroed by the ReLU, contributes nothing to reconstruction, and because it contributes nothing, the L1 penalty (which only penalizes active features) provides no gradient pressure to revive it, while the reconstruction loss also provides no gradient through a unit that's stuck at exactly zero output -- the unit is caught in a self-reinforcing dead zone with no training signal pushing it back to life, and 70% dead is a sign this happened at scale, often due to too-high an L1 coefficient or poor initialization that pushed many features negative simultaneously.

The diagnostic check is confirming this is genuinely a dead-feature problem rather than a correctly-sparse-but-functioning SAE: a well-functioning SAE should have most features firing rarely (sparse) but not zero across the entire evaluation set, so checking the actual per-feature activation-frequency histogram (not just a dead/alive binary count) distinguishes '70% of features fire on 0.1% of inputs' (expected, healthy sparsity) from '70% of features fire on literally zero inputs across the whole evaluation set' (dead).

The standard fix is periodic resampling of dead features during training: identify units that haven't fired in a recent window of training steps, and reinitialize their incoming weights (often biased toward directions in activation space that current reconstruction error is largest on, rather than purely random reinitialization), which gives them a fresh chance to find a useful role instead of staying permanently zeroed. Lowering the L1 coefficient and checking the initialization scale are also worth revisiting if resampling alone doesn't bring the dead rate down to a reasonable level, since a persistently very high dead rate after resampling often indicates the coefficient is still too aggressive for the chosen hidden dimension.
questions.professionalAnswer:

A feature that gets a negative pre-activation early on gets zeroed by the ReLU, contributes nothing to reconstruction, and because it's contributing nothing, the L1 penalty -- which only penalizes features that are actually active -- gives it zero gradient pressure to come back either. It's stuck in a self-reinforcing dead zone with no training signal pulling it back. 70% dead at this scale usually means the L1 coefficient was too aggressive, or the initialization pushed a lot of features negative all at once.

First thing I'd check is whether this is actually a dead-feature problem versus a correctly sparse SAE doing its job. A healthy SAE has most features firing rarely, not never -- so I'd pull the actual per-feature activation-frequency histogram, not just a binary dead/alive count, to tell apart '70% of features fire on 0.1% of inputs' (fine, that's sparsity working) from '70% fire on literally zero inputs across the whole eval set' (actually dead).

The standard fix is periodic resampling during training -- find units that haven't fired in some recent window of steps and reinitialize their incoming weights, ideally biased toward whatever directions currently have the largest reconstruction error rather than just random reinit, giving them an actual shot at a useful role instead of staying zeroed forever. If resampling alone doesn't bring the dead rate down to something reasonable, I'd revisit the L1 coefficient and the initialization scale directly -- a persistently high dead rate even after resampling usually means the coefficient is still too aggressive for the hidden dimension you picked.
commonMistakes: Not checking the actual activation-frequency histogram, confusing healthy sparsity with genuine dead features
Treating dead features as unfixable and just accepting the wasted capacity
Reinitializing dead features purely randomly instead of biasing toward high-reconstruction-error directions
Not revisiting the L1 coefficient when resampling alone fails to bring the dead rate down
keyPoints: Dead features arise from a ReLU/L1-penalty interaction with no gradient signal to revive a zeroed unit
Distinguishing dead features from healthy sparsity requires checking per-feature activation frequency, not a binary count
Periodic resampling of dead features, biased toward high-error directions, is the standard fix
A persistently high dead rate after resampling suggests the L1 coefficient or initialization needs adjustment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the ReLU/L1 dead-feature mechanism
Proposes checking activation-frequency distribution to confirm the diagnosis
Proposes feature resampling as the standard fix
Identifies L1 coefficient/initialization as a root-cause lever if resampling is insufficient

questions.title: A PPO Training Run Diverges as KL Explodes
questions.prompt: A PPO-based RLHF run is progressing normally, then the KL divergence from the reference policy starts growing rapidly, reward becomes erratic, and output quality visibly degrades within a few hundred steps. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
A rapid KL explosion with erratic reward and degrading quality is the signature of the policy update step size outrunning the KL constraint's ability to hold it in check, which can happen for a few distinct reasons that each point to a different fix: the KL coefficient itself may simply be set too low for the current reward scale, so the policy gradient term dominates and the KL penalty barely resists; the advantage estimates may have blown up in magnitude (a bug in GAE computation, or a reward scale that wasn't normalized, producing unusually large advantages that drive unusually large policy updates even with a correctly-sized KL coefficient); or the PPO clipping itself may not be functioning as intended due to an implementation bug (using the wrong old-policy log-probabilities, or not detaching them, causing the ratio calculation to be wrong).

The diagnostic order is checking each of these cheaply before assuming the worst: first confirm the KL coefficient's actual effective strength relative to the measured reward scale (is the reward-to-KL ratio in the objective wildly different from earlier in training, perhaps because reward-model scores for recently-generated outputs are larger in magnitude than they were earlier); second, log and inspect advantage magnitudes directly over the steps leading up to the explosion rather than inferring them from the aggregate loss; third, verify the PPO ratio computation specifically -- print or log the ratio distribution per step and confirm old-policy log-probabilities are frozen snapshots, not accidentally recomputed under the updated policy.

The immediate recovery action is restarting from the last checkpoint before the explosion began, since continuing to train past this point on a policy that's already drifted significantly tends to compound rather than self-correct. The fix going forward depends on which diagnostic above identified the cause: raising the KL coefficient and/or adding gradient clipping if it's a step-size issue, fixing the advantage computation or reward normalization if that's the source, or fixing the specific PPO implementation bug if the ratio calculation itself was wrong.

Rapid KL explosion with reward going erratic and quality visibly dropping within a few hundred steps is the signature of the policy update outrunning whatever's supposed to be constraining it, and there are a few distinct possible reasons that each point to a different fix. Maybe the KL coefficient is genuinely too low relative to the current reward scale, so the policy-gradient term is just dominating and the KL penalty barely pushes back. Maybe the advantage estimates themselves blew up -- a GAE bug, or unnormalized reward scale producing unusually large advantages that drive unusually large updates even with a reasonable KL coefficient. Or maybe the PPO clipping itself has a bug -- using the wrong old-policy log-probs, or not detaching them, which quietly breaks the ratio computation the whole clip depends on.

I'd check each of those cheaply in order rather than jumping to a conclusion. First, is the effective reward-to-KL balance in the objective actually different from earlier in training -- maybe reward-model scores for recent outputs got larger in magnitude for some unrelated reason. Second, I'd log advantage magnitudes directly over the steps right before the explosion, not infer them from the aggregate loss number. Third, I'd specifically verify the ratio computation -- log the ratio distribution per step and confirm the old-policy log-probs are genuinely frozen snapshots and not accidentally getting recomputed under the already-updated policy.

Immediately, I'd restart from the checkpoint before this started, because continuing to train on a policy that's already drifted this far tends to compound the problem rather than self-correct. What I actually change going forward depends entirely on which of those three checks turned up the cause -- raise the KL coefficient and add gradient clipping if it's a step-size issue, fix the advantage computation or reward normalization if that's it, or fix the specific implementation bug if the ratio calculation was wrong.

Continuing to train through the explosion rather than restarting from before it began
Only raising the KL coefficient without checking whether an advantage-computation or ratio bug is the real cause
Not logging advantage magnitudes directly, relying only on the aggregate loss to infer what happened
keyPoints: KL explosion can stem from too-low a KL coefficient, blown-up advantages, or a PPO ratio-computation bug
Diagnosis should check each cause cheaply and separately rather than guessing
Restarting from the pre-explosion checkpoint is the correct immediate recovery action
The long-term fix depends entirely on which specific cause the diagnosis identifies

Proposes a concrete, ordered diagnostic process for each cause
Proposes restarting from the pre-explosion checkpoint
Connects the fix to the specific diagnosed cause rather than a generic response

questions.title: A Query-Optimization RL Agent Exploits a Reward-Shaping Bug
questions.prompt: In the LTV AI Research Lab's query-plan-selection project, your RL agent's reward is improving dramatically, but when you inspect the actual execution plans it's choosing, several of them are objectively worse than the database optimizer's own choice, and the measured execution cost doesn't match what the reward implies. Diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer:
Reward improving while actual execution cost doesn't match what the reward implies points directly at a bug in how the reward is computed or measured, not the agent's policy -- the agent is faithfully optimizing whatever signal it's actually receiving, so the first place to look is the reward computation pipeline itself, specifically whether the 'actual cost' being measured is really what gets executed. A common concrete bug is measuring execution time or cost from a cached query result (the database serving a cached plan from a previous identical query rather than genuinely executing the hinted plan), which would make a bad plan look artificially cheap on repeat evaluation; another is a race condition where the cost measurement captures a concurrent query's resource usage rather than isolating the agent's own query.

The diagnostic step is re-running the suspicious high-reward episodes with caching explicitly disabled and with careful isolation from concurrent load, and comparing the freshly-measured cost against what the reward function recorded during training -- if the mismatch disappears under controlled re-measurement, the bug is confirmed to be in measurement, not in the agent's actual plan quality. It's also worth checking whether the relative-cost reward formulation (reward based on cost relative to the optimizer's own estimate) is using a stale or incorrectly-cached optimizer cost estimate rather than a freshly computed one for each query instance.

The fix requires disabling any caching in the execution-cost measurement path for RL training specifically (even if caching is desirable for production query serving, it corrupts the training signal here), adding an explicit isolation mechanism so concurrent load doesn't leak into a single episode's cost measurement, and re-running training from scratch (or from well before the bug's effects accumulated) once the measurement pipeline is fixed, since the policy has already been trained against a corrupted reward signal and cannot simply be patched going forward without retraining.
questions.professionalAnswer:

The agent is just faithfully optimizing whatever signal it's actually getting -- it's doing exactly what it was told to do. So I'd go look at the reward computation pipeline first, specifically whether 'actual cost' is really measuring what got executed. A really common concrete bug here is the database serving a cached result from a previous identical query instead of genuinely re-executing the hinted plan, which would make a bad plan look artificially cheap the second time around. To confirm, I'd re-run the suspicious high-reward episodes with caching explicitly disabled and genuinely isolated from any concurrent load, and compare that freshly-measured cost against whatever the reward function recorded during training. If the mismatch disappears under that controlled re-measurement, that confirms it's a measurement bug, not a real problem with the agent's plan choices. I'd also check whether the relative-cost reward -- cost relative to the optimizer's own estimate -- is pulling a stale or cached optimizer estimate instead of a freshly computed one per query.

The fix is disabling caching in the cost-measurement path specifically for RL training, even if caching is exactly what you want for production serving, because it's corrupting the training signal here. I'd add real isolation so concurrent load can't leak into one episode's measurement. And I'd retrain from scratch, or from well before the bug's effects built up -- the policy has already been trained against a corrupted signal, so patching the measurement going forward doesn't undo what it already learned from bad reward.

Not checking for cached query results making a bad plan look artificially cheap
Not checking for concurrent-load contamination in the cost measurement
Continuing training on the existing policy after fixing the bug instead of retraining from scratch or an earlier point

Caching of query results is a common concrete cause of artificially cheap-looking bad plans
Concurrent load contaminating cost measurement is another common isolation bug
Fixing the measurement bug requires retraining, since the existing policy was trained on corrupted reward

questions.title: The NL-to-SQL Assistant's Execution-Correctness Reward Gets Gamed by Safe Empty Queries
questions.prompt: In the LTV AI Research Lab's natural-language-to-SQL capstone, after an RLHF pass, the assistant's execution-correctness reward average has gone up, but a human spot-check shows it's increasingly generating overly narrow queries (adding extra WHERE conditions not asked for) that return empty or trivially small result sets which happen to avoid being penalized as wrong. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is reward hacking specific to how the execution-correctness reward handles the empty-result case: if empty or near-empty results aren't penalized harshly enough relative to a wrong-but-nonempty result (or worse, if an empty result is accidentally scored as a pass under a loose equality check against a sparse gold result), the policy discovers that narrowing a query with spurious extra conditions is a reliably safe way to avoid being penalized for a genuinely wrong, nonempty result, since an incorrect empty result is less obviously wrong than an incorrect nonempty one from the reward's point of view, even though it's equally or more unhelpful to a real user who asked a real question.

The diagnostic check is auditing the reward function's actual behavior on this specific failure pattern: construct test cases where the correct answer is a specific nonempty result, deliberately generate an overly-narrow query that returns empty, and confirm what reward value the function currently assigns -- if it's receiving zero (treated the same as any other near-miss) rather than a strong, explicit penalty, that confirms the exploit path. It's also worth checking whether this pattern correlates with prompts whose correct answer happens to involve a larger or more complex result set, since narrowing to empty is a lower-effort shortcut than correctly handling complex multi-condition queries.

The fix is making the reward function penalize an incorrect-and-empty result explicitly more harshly than an incorrect-and-nonempty result (reversing or at least flattening whatever made empty results a safer bet), and adding a specific regression check to the eval suite that measures the rate of empty-result outputs on prompts whose gold answer is known to be nonempty, tracked as its own metric during RL training rather than folded into the single aggregate reward number, so a recurrence of this exact pattern is caught early rather than discovered again via manual spot-check.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This is reward hacking specifically around how the execution-correctness reward handles empty results. If an empty result isn't penalized harder than a wrong-but-nonempty result -- or worse, if it's accidentally scored as a pass under some loose equality check against a sparse gold answer -- the policy will find that narrowing a query with extra conditions nobody asked for is a reliably safe way to dodge being penalized for a genuinely wrong nonempty result. An incorrect empty result just looks less obviously wrong to the reward function than an incorrect nonempty one, even though it's equally useless or worse to an actual user.

To confirm, I'd build test cases where I know the correct answer is a specific nonempty result, deliberately generate an overly-narrow query that comes back empty, and check exactly what reward that gets today. If it's scoring as a plain zero -- same as any other near-miss -- instead of a real, explicit penalty, that's the exploit confirmed. I'd also check whether this pattern shows up more on prompts where the correct answer involves a bigger or more complex result set, since narrowing to empty is a much lower-effort shortcut than actually handling a complicated multi-condition query correctly.

The fix is making the reward explicitly penalize incorrect-and-empty harder than incorrect-and-nonempty, so empty stops being the safe bet it currently is. And I'd add a dedicated metric to the eval suite -- specifically the rate of empty-result outputs on prompts where the gold answer is known to be nonempty -- tracked on its own during RL training, not folded into one aggregate reward number, so this exact pattern gets caught by monitoring next time instead of needing a human to notice it in a spot-check again.

Missing that this is a reward-design gap, not a model-capability gap (the model isn't failing to understand the query)
Not adding a dedicated empty-result-rate metric, relying only on manual spot-checks to catch recurrence
Fixing the immediate instance without checking whether the pattern correlates with harder, more complex queries
keyPoints: The exploit works because empty results aren't penalized more harshly than wrong-but-nonempty results
Confirm by directly testing the reward function's score on a known-nonempty-answer case made artificially empty
The fix explicitly makes incorrect-and-empty worse than incorrect-and-nonempty in the reward

questions.title: A Checkpoint Resume Produces a Loss Spike That the Original Run Didn't Have
questions.prompt: A long training run was paused and resumed from a checkpoint for scheduled maintenance. After resuming, the loss spikes sharply for several hundred steps before settling back down, something that didn't happen at that point in an earlier, uninterrupted test run on the same data order. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
A loss spike specifically at a checkpoint resume boundary, absent in an otherwise-identical uninterrupted run, points at something checkpoint-specific not being restored correctly, most commonly optimizer state -- a checkpoint that saves model weights but not the optimizer's momentum/variance buffers (or the learning-rate scheduler's internal step counter) effectively restarts those as if training were beginning from scratch, even though the model weights themselves are far along, which causes a genuine mismatch between where the weights are and what the optimizer 'thinks' it knows about recent gradient history, producing exactly this kind of transient destabilization that then settles once the optimizer state re-accumulates enough history.

The diagnostic check is auditing exactly what the checkpoint saves and confirming optimizer state and scheduler state are both included and were both actually loaded on resume, not just the model weights -- a common and specific bug is a checkpoint-saving function that was written for model weights only and never updated when the optimizer was changed to one with meaningful state (Adam's momentum and variance estimates matter far more here than, say, plain SGD would). Also worth checking: whether the data loader's position/shuffling state was correctly restored, since resuming with the model at step N but the data loader accidentally restarting from the beginning of an epoch would reintroduce already-seen data in a different order, which can also cause a transient disturbance though with a different signature than an optimizer-state issue.

The fix is correcting the checkpoint save/load logic to include full optimizer and scheduler state, verifying this with a direct test (save a checkpoint, resume from it immediately with no gap, and confirm the loss curve is smooth with no artificial discontinuity), and re-running the incident resume from the last good checkpoint once confirmed fixed, since training through the bug-induced spike likely still has some lasting effect on the current run's trajectory worth being cautious about.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A loss spike specifically right at the resume boundary, that an otherwise identical uninterrupted run didn't have, points at something checkpoint-specific not getting restored properly -- and the usual suspect is optimizer state. If the checkpoint saves model weights but not the optimizer's momentum and variance buffers, or the scheduler's internal step counter, resuming effectively restarts those as if training were beginning fresh, even though the weights themselves are far along. That mismatch between where the weights actually are and what the optimizer 'remembers' about recent gradients is exactly the kind of thing that produces a transient spike that settles once the optimizer re-accumulates history.

First thing I'd audit is exactly what the checkpoint function saves, and confirm optimizer and scheduler state are both in there and both actually got loaded on resume, not just the weights. This is a specific, common bug -- a checkpoint function written back when the setup used an optimizer with no real state, never updated when the team moved to Adam, where the momentum and variance estimates matter a lot more. I'd also check the data loader's position and shuffling state -- if the model resumed at step N but the data loader restarted from the beginning of an epoch, you'd get a transient disturbance too, just with a different signature than an optimizer-state bug.

Fix is correcting the save/load logic to include full optimizer and scheduler state, and I wouldn't just trust the fix -- I'd verify it directly: save a checkpoint, resume immediately with zero gap, and confirm the loss curve is smooth with no artificial discontinuity at all. Once that's confirmed, I'd re-run the actual incident resume from the last good checkpoint rather than just continuing past the spike, since training through a bug-induced spike probably had some lasting effect on the run worth not just shrugging off.

Not checking whether optimizer and scheduler state, not just model weights, were saved and restored
Not verifying the fix with a direct zero-gap save-then-resume test before trusting it
Continuing to train through the bug-induced spike instead of re-running the resume once the bug is fixed
keyPoints: A resume-specific spike points to missing optimizer/scheduler state in the checkpoint, not random noise
Adam-style optimizers are especially sensitive to lost momentum/variance state on resume
Data loader position/shuffling state is a separate thing to verify alongside optimizer state
The fix should be verified with a direct zero-gap save/resume test before trusting it in production

Proposes auditing exactly what the checkpoint saves/restores
Proposes a concrete verification test for the fix
Proposes re-running the affected resume rather than continuing past the spike

questions.title: An Ablation Comparison Is Confounded by an Unlisted Hyperparameter Difference
questions.prompt: Two ablation runs meant to isolate the effect of a single architecture change show a meaningful difference in final loss, and a teammate wants to write up the architecture change as the cause. You suspect the comparison might be confounded. What do you check before signing off on the conclusion?
questions.modelAnswer:
A clean ablation needs every setting except the one variable under test to be identical between the two runs, and the most common way this breaks is an unlisted or assumed-identical hyperparameter that actually differs -- the first check is a literal, line-by-line diff of both runs' full configs (not just the ones someone remembers setting), since a config management issue (a default value that changed between when run A and run B were launched, a seed that wasn't explicitly pinned and defaulted differently, a learning-rate warmup length that was tied to a now-different total step count) is a far more common cause of a measured difference than the intended architecture change.

The second check is confirming both runs actually used the same data order and the same random seed for data shuffling and initialization, since a different seed alone can produce a measurable difference in final loss on its own, especially for runs that aren't trained to full convergence -- if seed wasn't explicitly controlled and matched, the observed gap could be entirely attributable to seed variance rather than the architecture change, and the only way to know is running the comparison across multiple seeds for both arms and checking whether the architecture-change effect is still present and consistent across them, not just a single comparison.

If the config diff and seed check come back clean, the next step before accepting the conclusion is checking the effect size against the measured run-to-run variance from repeated runs of the same configuration (if available) -- a difference comparable to normal seed-to-seed noise shouldn't be reported as a real architecture effect regardless of how clean the rest of the setup is. Only after all of this is a conclusion that the architecture change caused the observed difference actually supportable, and the writeup should explicitly state what was checked, not just report the final numbers.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A clean ablation needs everything except the one thing you're testing to be identical, and the way this breaks most often isn't some subtle statistical issue -- it's a config difference nobody noticed. So first thing I do is a literal, line-by-line diff of the full configs for both runs, not just the settings someone remembers deciding on, because a default value that changed between when the two runs were launched, an unpinned seed that defaulted differently, or a warmup length that happened to be tied to a different total step count are all far more common explanations for a measured gap than the actual architecture change.

Second, I'd specifically confirm both runs used the same data order and the same seed for shuffling and initialization. A different seed alone can produce a real, measurable difference in final loss, especially if the runs aren't trained all the way to convergence. If seed wasn't explicitly pinned and matched, I wouldn't trust the comparison at all -- the real test is running both arms across multiple seeds and checking whether the architecture effect holds up consistently, not relying on one single comparison that could just be seed noise.

If the config diff and the seed check both come back clean, the last thing I'd check is whether the effect size is actually bigger than normal run-to-run variance, using repeated runs of the same config if we have them. A gap that's within normal seed-to-seed noise shouldn't get written up as a real architecture effect no matter how clean everything else looks. Only once all three of those check out would I sign off on the conclusion, and I'd want the writeup to actually say what was checked, not just show the final two numbers side by side.
commonMistakes: Comparing two runs' final numbers without diffing their full configs line by line
Not checking whether both runs used the same seed and data order
Drawing a conclusion from a single comparison instead of checking the effect across multiple seeds
Not comparing the effect size against known run-to-run variance before accepting it as real

questions.title: An Activation-Patching Effect Appears on Toy Data but Vanishes at Scale
questions.prompt: You validated a circuit on a small, custom-trained toy transformer using activation patching, with a strong, clean effect. When you attempt the same patching procedure on a larger, more capable model trained on real data, the effect is much weaker and noisier, even for seemingly analogous prompts. Diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer:
A clean toy-model circuit weakening at scale is a well-documented pattern with several plausible, non-mutually-exclusive explanations that need to be checked rather than assumed: larger models often distribute a given computation across more redundant pathways (multiple heads or layers contributing partially to the same function, a consequence of superposition and the larger capacity available), so patching a single location recovers less of the effect simply because no single location carries the whole computation anymore, unlike a toy model trained with just enough capacity for one clean mechanism. Checking whether patching multiple candidate locations jointly (rather than one at a time) recovers more of the effect is the direct test of this redundancy hypothesis.

A second explanation is that the toy model was trained on a narrow, templated data distribution specifically designed to elicit the behavior cleanly, while the larger model trained on diverse real data may implement the same surface behavior via a different, less uniform mechanism across different input types -- the same output behavior doesn't guarantee the same underlying circuit, especially once the input distribution is far more varied than what produced the toy-model finding. This is checked by stratifying the larger model's test prompts by surface features and seeing whether the patching effect is strong for some subsets and weak for others, rather than uniformly weak, which would suggest the mechanism is real but input-dependent rather than simply absent.

A third, more mundane explanation worth ruling out early is a straightforward implementation mismatch -- the layer indexing, head indexing, or exact hook placement that worked for the toy model's specific architecture may not map correctly onto the larger model's architecture (different layer normalization placement, different numbers of heads, a different attention implementation), producing a patch that's technically running but at a subtly wrong location. Confirming hook placement against the larger model's actual architecture documentation, not assuming the toy-model code ports over directly, should be checked before concluding anything about redundancy or distribution differences.
